newsitem.title: USA: New law challenges small U.S. investment advisers.
newsitem.headline: New law challenges small U.S. investment advisers.

text.p: Small registered investment adviser (RIA) firms face a period of growing pains after sweeping reform of regulations signed last month by President Bill Clinton, some advisers said Wednesday.

The new law divides jurisdiction of registered investment advisers between the states and the federal Securities and Exchange Commission based on the size of assets under management. Advisers with more than $25 million in assets under management and advisers to mutual funds will continue to be regulated by the SEC. Firms with less than $25 million under management will be regulated exclusively by individual states.
The law was changed to relieve the regulatory burden on the SEC and streamline rules to protect customers.
While many welcome the RIA reforms, some small advisers complained at an industry conference here that state supervision puts them at a disadvantage.
"I am certainly nursing the hope that Congress will revisit this," said Charles Rice, an investment adviser from St. Louis, Mo.
Rice and others said that dividing the industry into two tiers of regulation was unfair for the small adviser.
"We are all very unhappy about the marketing implications," Rice said. "Who would you rather have regulate your advisers, the SEC or the state?"

In many cases, state laws on investment advisers only fill in where federal rules leave off, leaving the industry and the states to rewrite regulations on the state level, said Dee Harris, president of the North American Securities Administrators Association.
"We have six months to sort it out with the SEC" before the new law becomes effective, Harris said. President Clinton signed the bill October 11. It takes effect 180 days from then.
But in the meantime, small advisers may face slack supervision and confusion, and they prefer SEC regulation, adviser Rice said.
"Probably 99 percent of the small money managers can't stand this bifurcation," Rice said. "They want to see a unified plan."
Iowa, Wyoming, Colorado and Ohio currently do not have investment adviser laws, so supervision of advisers in those states remains with the SEC.

"The sweeping overhaul really benefitted the big firms, while small firms are really challenged under the legislation," agreed Peter Mauthe, president of the Society of Asset Allocators and Fund Timers, the group holding the conference.
The larger firms no longer have to register with individual states and also have the marketing advantage of touting the fact that they are SEC-regulated.
Smaller firms, on the other hand, need to register with individual states, which often have varying rules, making it difficult for the funds to operate in more than one state.
But overall, Mauthe said streamlining the legislation was a step forward.
"Now we have to go back to work and get clarification on certain issues," Mauthe said. -Chris Romans (312) 408-8750
